content: Stage fright, also known as performance anxiety, is a condition characterized by anxiety, fear, or a persistent phobia associated with performing in front of an audience or a camera. This type of anxiety can occur before or during any activity that involves public self-presentation. The term stage fright or topophobia is often confused with glossophobia, which specifically refers to the fear of public speaking. However, the distinction becomes clear when considering performers such as jugglers and mimes, who may experience performance anxiety without necessarily engaging in public speaking. Performance anxiety is also observed in athletes, where it is interpreted as a fear of underperforming, either in front of an actual audience or due to the implied pressure of public scrutiny. Stage fright frequently arises in anticipation of a performance, sometimes occurring long before the event itself. It manifests in various physical and psychological symptoms, including a fluttering or pounding heart, trembling in the hands and legs, diarrhea, facial nerve tics, and dry mouth. This condition can affect individuals across a wide spectrum, from ordinary people and novice performers to highly accomplished artists. Some musicians manage stage fright by using beta blockers to mitigate symptoms during auditions and performances. In other cases, performers resort to consuming alcoholic beverages to alleviate their anxiety. However, this practice has, in numerous instances, led to the development of alcoholism.
